name: 35th Annual Conference of the British Association for Cardiovascular Prevention and Rehabilitation: Reshaping the Future of Cardiovascular Prevention and Rehabilitation
description: The BACPR annual conference programme covers cardiovascular prevention and rehabilitation, with keynote presentations, workshops, oral abstracts, posters, and sessions on service delivery and workforce development.

notes.title: Time to adjust our focus? How environmental risks to cardiovascular health challenge our paradigm of individual cardiovascular disease prevention and management
notes.summary:
OVERVIEW
The speaker argues that cardiovascular prevention should retain its focus on individual risk factors while also giving greater attention to environmental risks, including air pollution, noise, and extreme temperatures. The talk reviews proposed mechanisms and evidence, discusses patient-facing advice, and calls for clinician advocacy for population-level action.

MAIN ARGUMENTS
• Individual prevention—such as addressing blood pressure, cholesterol, smoking, diet, and physical activity—has been successful and should continue.
• A focus on risks under individual control can leave environmental exposures under-addressed, despite their contribution to cardiovascular disease.
• Environmental and individual factors interact; the speaker uses the exposome concept to connect health with social, built, and environmental conditions.
• Clinical advice can help individuals, but reducing environmental hazards also requires systemic and population-wide measures. Clinicians can contribute through advocacy.

KEY FINDINGS
• The speaker describes a Global Burden of Disease analysis ranking 15 leading cardiovascular risk factors, six of which were characterized as environmental. Air pollution, lead exposure, and extreme temperatures were among them. The speaker reports that air pollution accounts for more cardiovascular death and disability than smoking.
• Fine particulate matter (PM2.5) is presented as the air-pollution component most strongly associated with cardiovascular disease. A U.S. study of nearly 60 million people aged 65 or older found an association between higher chronic ambient PM2.5 exposure and first cardiovascular hospital admission, including across the study’s reported low exposure range.
• A multi-country analysis of more than 30 million cardiovascular deaths found higher cardiovascular mortality at extreme cold and hot temperatures.
• The talk describes proposed pathways including oxidative stress, inflammation, autonomic effects, endothelial dysfunction, vasoconstriction, and altered clotting. Noise and temperature exposures are also described as having cardiovascular effects through stress, sleep disruption, dehydration, or vasoconstriction.

METHODS OR EVIDENCE
• The talk summarizes a Global Burden of Disease analysis using data on deaths and disability collected since 1990 across 204 countries.
• It refers to a joint environmental-risk statement from the European Society of Cardiology, American College of Cardiology, American Heart Association, and World Heart Federation. The statement groups environmental risks into domains including air pollution, climate change, noise and light, and water, soil, and chemical pollution.
• The PM2.5 example was a U.S. study of adults aged 65 or older, covering 2000–2016, with chronic exposure assessed over three years and first hospital admissions examined.
• The temperature example analyzed daily cardiovascular deaths in more than 500 cities across 27 countries and five continents over about 40 years.
• The talk also cites mechanistic explanations and the World Heart Federation’s Air Pollution and Heart Health Toolkit. Full study citations and detailed methods are not provided in the transcript.

PRACTICAL OR CLINICAL IMPLICATIONS
• Ask patients about potential indoor and outdoor air-pollution exposure, including solid-fuel use and proximity to industry or heavy traffic.
• Discuss locally available air-quality information and alerts. The speaker describes reducing exposure during poor-air-quality periods, including staying indoors or closing windows when appropriate and avoiding outdoor exercise during high pollution.
• For regular exposure to poor outdoor air quality, the speaker says personal protection such as an FFP2/N95 mask may be recommended. For indoor pollution, possible measures depend on the source and can include ventilation, filtration, or switching to cleaner energy.
• Continue managing conventional cardiovascular risks, which the speaker says may reduce overall susceptibility to pollution-related cardiovascular events.
• For broader environmental hazards, clinicians can educate and signpost patients and advocate for population-wide policies and regulation.

LIMITATIONS AND UNCERTAINTIES
• The transcript provides no full bibliographic references, detailed study methods, or numerical uncertainty estimates, limiting independent assessment of the cited evidence.
• The examples described are largely observational associations; the talk does not establish that the reported exposure–outcome relationships are causal in each study.
• The transcript does not discuss in detail the effectiveness, suitability, or potential trade-offs of each individual exposure-reduction measure.
• No audience discussion or question-and-answer exchange is included in the transcript.

AUDIENCE QUESTIONS
No audience questions are included in the transcript.

FOLLOW-UP READING
• The joint environmental-risk statement from the European Society of Cardiology, American College of Cardiology, American Heart Association, and World Heart Federation, as referenced in the talk.
• The World Heart Federation’s Air Pollution and Heart Health Toolkit for healthcare professionals.
• The Global Burden of Cardiovascular Disease Collaboration analysis discussed in the talk. Full publication details were not provided.

notes.title: Introducing Compassionate Mindful Resilience Course as part of Cardiac Rehab – Feedback from patient evaluation and outcome measure
notes.summary:
OVERVIEW
The chief therapist from South Manchester Cardiac Rehab presented a pilot of an accredited four-week Compassionate Mindful Resilience course delivered as part of cardiac rehabilitation, including patient feedback and evaluation of an outcome measure.

MAIN ARGUMENTS
The course was selected for its brief mindfulness interventions, which were intended to be manageable for patients. The speaker reported that patients enjoyed the course and that the pilot showed significant pre- to post-course change on the cardiac distress measure.

KEY FINDINGS
The speaker reported a statistically significant difference in pre- and post-course Cardiac Distress Inventory Structured Short Form (CDI-SF) scores among the 18 people who completed the evaluation; score values were not provided in the transcript. Patient feedback suggested that participants perceived greater acceptance of their cardiac condition and less fear. Participants also described practices they continued to use. The speaker characterized the course as having significant changes in “social health.”

METHODS OR EVIDENCE
The course consisted of four weekly sessions of about two hours, with short practices (around 10 minutes) and recorded material for home practice between sessions. The speaker reported running four or five courses: one online and four face-to-face. There were 27 participants in total, 21 course completers, and 18 evaluation respondents. Evidence included pre- and post-course CDI-SF scores and patient-perception questions and comments.

PRACTICAL OR CLINICAL IMPLICATIONS
The pilot suggests this short-practice course can be delivered within cardiac rehabilitation and was well received by participants. The speaker noted that participant completion and evaluation response were learning points for future delivery.

LIMITATIONS AND UNCERTAINTIES
This was described as a pilot. The transcript does not give the CDI-SF scores, effect size, statistical test, exact significance level, or detailed feedback results. Reasons for non-completion were mentioned but not specified. The number of courses is reported as four or five, and no further detail is provided about participant characteristics or follow-up.

AUDIENCE QUESTIONS
No audience questions were included in the transcript.

FOLLOW-UP READING
No follow-up reading was mentioned.

notes.title: Finding Time for Research in Real-World Clinical Practice: Honest Conversations from the Front Line
notes.summary:
OVERVIEW
A panel discussion about how clinicians and academics can make research more achievable and connected to clinical practice, particularly in cardiac rehabilitation and cardiovascular care. Conference, formal talk title, and speaker details were not provided.

MAIN ARGUMENTS
- Research needs to be treated as part of clinical work, with protected time reflected in job plans, appraisals, or professional development plans.
- A supportive research culture can grow through journal clubs, research champions, mentoring, collaboration, and small starting projects such as audits, service evaluations, or abstracts.
- Clinical-academic partnerships work best when built early, including discussion of study feasibility, ethics, data access, and the service’s needs.
- Research engagement should support safe, effective, evidence-based care and account for clinician expertise and patient preferences.

KEY FINDINGS
Panelists described research involvement developing from postgraduate study, clinical roles, and personal interests. Examples of research or evaluation informing practice included a breathlessness rehabilitation programme developed from research involving people with respiratory disease and heart failure, and service evaluation or audit work connected with cardiac rehabilitation delivery and referrals. One panelist reported an increase in referrals to exercise programmes in annual audit data, but no figures or study details were given.

METHODS OR EVIDENCE
The discussion drew on panelists’ professional experiences rather than presenting a formal study or systematic review. Examples included journal clubs, MSc projects, audits, service evaluations, research abstracts, a PhD concerning spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD), and cross-university student projects. The transcript gives no formal methods, sample sizes, statistical results, or references for these examples.

PRACTICAL OR CLINICAL IMPLICATIONS
- Schedule and protect time for research or scholarship, and raise it with managers through appraisal or development planning.
- Start with manageable activities and seek colleagues with complementary research skills.
- Use research champions and regular academic-clinical contact to shape feasible projects early.
- Explore local university links, student projects, mentoring, and professional-body networks; clarify ethics, data-sharing, and contracts before collecting data.
- Share service findings and explain their relevance to care and service development.

LIMITATIONS AND UNCERTAINTIES
This was a panel discussion, not a report of a single research study. The examples were described briefly and without enough detail to assess their design, quality, or effects. No specific funding routes, contacts, publications, or completed outcome data were supplied. Some organization names and acronyms in the transcript are unclear, and the transcript ends mid-thought.

AUDIENCE QUESTIONS
Audience members asked how academics can make studies workable for clinical services; how clinicians can pursue research when teams lack time or encouragement; how to find collaborators and suitable funding; whether students can help with data collection; and how to manage ethics, data sharing, and contracts. They also asked for examples of research translated into practice and suggested creating university-service links and identifying services ready to take part in studies.

FOLLOW-UP READING
No specific publications were cited. The panel mentioned Scotland’s “Transforming Roles” paper in relation to protected learning time, and referred to the BACPR website, mentoring, and research-support resources. These were discussed as possible resources; no links or full citations were provided.
notes.speaker: Dr Sheona McHale, Marissa Plaza and Kirsty Hughes (hosts; individual panel speakers not listed)

notes.title: Practical implementation of a GLP-1 RA in adults with established cardiovascular disease (CVD) and BMI ≥27 kg/m²
notes.summary:
OVERVIEW
The talk discussed semaglutide (Wegovy) for cardiovascular risk reduction in adults with established cardiovascular disease who are overweight or obese, alongside diet and physical activity. Speakers identified themselves as Nick Bower and Nadeesh Khan; the conference and official talk title were not supplied.

MAIN ARGUMENTS
Semaglutide may offer additional cardiovascular risk reduction for patients whose conventional secondary-prevention risk factors are already treated. The speakers emphasized that its cardiovascular role is distinct from prescribing it solely for diabetes or weight loss, and that patients need ongoing support during treatment.

KEY FINDINGS
The presenters reported that SELECT found a 20% reduction in cardiovascular risk with semaglutide. They cited 569 three-point MACE events in the semaglutide group versus 701 with placebo over approximately 40 months. The stated endpoint comprised cardiovascular death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, or stroke. They said cardiovascular benefit could appear before substantial weight loss.

METHODS OR EVIDENCE
SELECT was described as a cardiovascular outcomes trial involving more than 17,500 patients across 41 countries. The speakers described eligibility as age over 45, established cardiovascular disease, BMI of at least 27, and no prior diabetes. Treatment was titrated from 0.25 mg at four-week intervals toward a 2.4 mg maintenance dose. The presenters also referred to NICE guidance, but gave no full citation or detailed recommendation text.

PRACTICAL OR CLINICAL IMPLICATIONS
The speakers advised gradual, individualized dose escalation, pausing or returning to a previously tolerated dose when side effects warrant it rather than rushing to 2.4 mg. They discussed dietary adjustments, smaller frequent meals for nausea, hydration, and physical activity. They highlighted muscle loss as a concern and recommended attention to protein intake and strength training. They also advised caution regarding diabetic retinopathy, referral for visual disturbances, and consideration of temporarily pausing some cardiovascular medicines during significant vomiting or diarrhoea. They stressed continued follow-up rather than simply handing care back to primary care.

LIMITATIONS AND UNCERTAINTIES
The transcript does not provide full trial references, statistical details, or the exact NICE recommendation. The speakers could not give the audience an exact figure for muscle loss or confirm the specific body-composition data from SELECT. They said there were no specific routine blood-test monitoring suggestions for semaglutide, while recommending assessment of relevant comorbidities and risk factors. They also noted uncertainty about whether semaglutide affects absorption of other medicines. The talk’s efficacy and safety claims are presented as the speakers’ account of trial evidence.

AUDIENCE QUESTIONS
Questions covered muscle loss and exercise, blood-test monitoring, body-composition results from SELECT, persistent burning or tingling sensations, and possible effects on cardiovascular medicines or their absorption. For persistent unusual sensory symptoms, the speakers suggested considering dose reduction or stopping treatment if symptoms continued. They could not provide the exact muscle-loss data during the session.

FOLLOW-UP READING
No full publications or citations were provided in the transcript. The speakers recommended patient resources from the British Heart Foundation and Heart UK for dietary advice.

notes.title: Too Young for Cardiac Rehabilitation? Rethinking Support for Children and Young People with Heart Conditions
notes.summary:
OVERVIEW
The talk challenged the assumption that children with heart conditions do not need cardiac rehabilitation. It described evidence gaps in existing pediatric programs and a co-developed program, CardioActive, then reported findings from a randomized feasibility trial.

MAIN ARGUMENTS
Children and young people with heart conditions can face physical, psychological, and social challenges, despite improved survival. Rehabilitation may therefore need to combine exercise, education, and mental health support. The speaker argued that interventions should be based on theory and co-developed with young people.

KEY FINDINGS
A systematic review included 44 studies: 70% offered exercise alone, and few combined exercise, education, and psychological support. Seventy percent reportedly had no theoretical basis. The review and its meta-analysis were still ongoing.

CardioActive is a six-weekly-session program, with each session lasting 90 minutes. In its feasibility trial, 100 young people were recruited, and the three stated progression criteria were met: recruitment to target, follow-up questionnaire return of at least 80%, and qualitative evidence about acceptability. Participants attended an average of at least four of six sessions, and therapist adherence to the program manual was reported as 99.5%.

The speaker reported improvements in psychological and quality-of-life measures in the CardioActive arm, particularly around emotional symptoms, and positive trends on walking tests. These are preliminary feasibility findings, not definitive evidence of effectiveness. Interviews with 20 participants identified the value of the hospital setting, peer support, increased confidence, and perceived psychological and behavioral changes. Participants recommended the program and some wanted it to last longer.

METHODS OR EVIDENCE
The talk combined an ongoing systematic review and meta-analysis with a single-blind randomized feasibility trial comparing CardioActive with treatment as usual. The trial included young people aged 11–16 and assessed them at baseline, three months, and six months. Young people considered at significant suicide risk or at exercise risk were excluded. Measures included psychological and quality-of-life questionnaires, walking tests, and activity monitoring; activity-monitor data had not yet been analyzed. Qualitative interviews were conducted with 20 participants.

PRACTICAL OR CLINICAL IMPLICATIONS
A theory-informed, group-based program that integrates exercise, education, and psychological support appears feasible and acceptable in the reported setting. Peer contact and supported exercise may help young people feel safer, more confident, and less limited by concerns about symptoms. Any exercise advice should remain appropriate to an individual's clinical risk and specialist assessment.

LIMITATIONS AND UNCERTAINTIES
This was a feasibility trial, not a full-scale effectiveness trial; the reported outcome differences should be treated as preliminary. The speaker noted that some outcome measures may not be sensitive or tailored enough for this population, follow-up was limited to six months, and activity-monitor data were not yet analyzed. Longer-term outcomes, cost-effectiveness, and health-economic results remain unknown. The review and meta-analysis were incomplete, and results for some combined-program categories were not yet available. The transcript does not provide full adverse-event details or bibliographic citations.

AUDIENCE QUESTIONS
No audience questions are included in the transcript.

FOLLOW-UP READING
The speaker said the systematic review protocol had been published, but gave no title or citation. Further results from the ongoing review and analyses were expected to be reported later; no specific references were provided.

notes.title: Connected Hearts: Extending Cardiac Rehab beyond the Programme
notes.summary:
OVERVIEW
The speaker described Connected Hearts, a quarterly digital newsletter for people after cardiac rehabilitation. It aims to support the transition from supervised rehab to ongoing self-management through repeated prompts and signposting to trusted resources and local community activities.

MAIN ARGUMENTS
- Completing cardiac rehabilitation does not mean lifestyle changes are established; motivation and routines may falter after structured support ends.
- Continued, repeated reminders and accessible opportunities may help people sustain healthy choices.
- Post-rehab support need not require a new clinic or complex technology: an email newsletter using existing resources can offer a simple way to stay connected.

KEY FINDINGS
- After one year, 56 cardiac rehab graduates responded to an online survey, reported as a 60% response rate.
- 93% said the newsletter would help motivate them to address lifestyle changes; 97% said it would help them continue.
- Respondents included older adults: 25% were aged 70–79 and 15% aged 80–89.
- The speaker described the project as having no cost, using existing resources, and requiring minimal staff time.

METHODS OR EVIDENCE
The project sends quarterly digital newsletters to cardiac rehab graduates. Newsletters reinforce secondary prevention and signpost to local walking groups, community exercise and activity groups, wellbeing resources, and support services. Patient feedback was gathered through an online survey one year after the project began. The reported percentages reflect respondents’ perceptions, not measured behavior change.

PRACTICAL OR CLINICAL IMPLICATIONS
Cardiac rehab teams could consider maintaining contact after discharge with brief, recurring messages and practical links to local supports. The speaker also emphasized inviting patients to participate alongside staff in community activities, rather than only advising them to become more active.

LIMITATIONS AND UNCERTAINTIES
The evidence described is a survey of 56 respondents, with a 60% response rate. The outcomes reported were perceptions of potential motivation and continuation, not observed lifestyle behavior or clinical outcomes. The transcript provides no comparison group, detailed survey methods, or longer-term outcome data, so the project’s effect on behavior or health cannot be determined from this account.

AUDIENCE QUESTIONS
No audience questions are included in the transcript.

FOLLOW-UP READING
No follow-up reading or references were provided in the transcript.

notes.title: The burden of undiagnosed and undertreated modifiable cardiovascular risk in England: national and small area prevalence estimates from the Health Survey for England
notes.summary:
OVERVIEW
The talk described a project to estimate the prevalence and geographic distribution of five modifiable cardiovascular risk factors across England, including risk that is not captured in diagnosed-condition data.

MAIN ARGUMENTS
Knowing where risk factors are present—including when they are undiagnosed—is necessary to target prevention. The speaker cited the potential to prevent much cardiovascular disease by addressing modifiable risks and presented small-area estimates as a way to identify unmet need.

KEY FINDINGS
The analysis estimated that 17 million people in England have hypertension, with substantial gaps in diagnosis and control; the speaker’s breakdown of these categories was unclear. Hypertension was highest in rural and coastal areas and lowest in urban and student areas. Dyslipidemia affected 46% of adults, was mostly untreated, and was more evenly distributed geographically.

The 2021 smoking estimate was 12.7%; the speaker said a more recent estimate was about 9.5%. Smoking remained concentrated in deprived urban areas in the north and in parts of London. An estimated 14% of adults had prediabetes, while 1.5 million people (3.2% of adults) had diabetes without knowing it; most people with diabetes were said to be above their HbA1c target. About one-third of adults had normal BMI, one-third were overweight, and one-third were obese, with overweight and obesity patterned by deprivation and more common in northern and urban areas.

Across the population, 62% of adults were estimated to have one risk factor, 24% two, and 6% three or more.

METHODS OR EVIDENCE
The project used 11 years of Health Survey for England data covering 87,000 people. The survey samples households and includes interviews, home visits, measured height and weight, repeated blood-pressure measurements, and blood tests. The researchers used survey-weighted analyses to produce national prevalence estimates using 2021 data, built models, and applied them to 2021 census data to predict small-area patterns. Existing data were described as insufficient because they capture diagnosed risk factors.

PRACTICAL OR CLINICAL IMPLICATIONS
An interactive web-based data explorer was being prepared to help users examine risk in local practice areas. The stated next steps were to make the data publicly available and design a pilot targeted intervention for populations with the greatest need.

LIMITATIONS AND UNCERTAINTIES
The estimates are model-based small-area predictions, rather than direct measurements of every local population. The speaker referred to a slide on strengths and weaknesses but did not describe them in the transcript. Some spoken figures or category descriptions were unclear, including the hypertension breakdown. The transcript gives no detailed model specifications or uncertainty estimates.

AUDIENCE QUESTIONS
No audience questions were recorded; the session moved on because the program was behind schedule.

FOLLOW-UP READING
The talk named the Health Survey for England and the 2021 Census as data sources but provided no citations, links, or further reading details.

notes.title: The exploration of lived experiences and the associated relationship with physical activity and exercise for individuals with ANOCA
notes.summary:
OVERVIEW
Kayleigh Jara, a Master’s by Research student at the University of Aberdeen, presented a project exploring the health experiences of people with ANOCA (angina with non-obstructive coronary arteries) and how the condition affects their relationship with physical activity and exercise.

MAIN ARGUMENTS
Participants described symptoms that were unpredictable and sometimes intense, making physical activity feel risky and difficult to sustain. The speaker argued that these experiences, alongside limited awareness of ANOCA and inconsistent healthcare advice, point to a need for more personalised exercise support.

KEY FINDINGS
• Participants reported symptoms at rest, during activity, and sometimes after exertion. Chest pain and breathlessness were common; fatigue, nausea, brain fog, dizziness, and back or neck pain were also described.
• Fear of provoking symptoms, being hospitalised, having a heart attack, or dying contributed to reduced activity, including changes in its frequency, intensity, and duration.
• Participants described individual heart-rate thresholds for symptoms, usually around 120 beats per minute, with reported thresholds ranging from 80 to 145. They also said prolonged or intense activity could worsen symptoms.
• Post-exercise symptoms could begin about two hours after activity and last hours to days. Household tasks and social events, as well as exercise, could trigger symptoms and require recovery time.
• Participants reported lengthy or difficult diagnostic journeys, dismissal or misattribution of symptoms, and conflicting exercise advice. Some turned to smartwatches, AI, and social-media support groups for information or support.
• Early co-design discussions indicated a strong desire for personalised exercise prescriptions. Participants requested online options that accommodate unpredictable symptoms, self-pacing, and rest.

METHODS OR EVIDENCE
The speaker described a three-stage project that included focus groups with experienced clinicians and focus groups with people with ANOCA. Patient discussions were conducted online as semi-structured sessions, with three to six people per group and sessions lasting up to two hours. Topics included exercise structure, warm-ups, activity type, and safety parameters. The patient focus groups had finished the week before the talk, so the findings presented were initial and based on participant self-report.

PRACTICAL OR CLINICAL IMPLICATIONS
The accounts suggest that exercise guidance may need to be individualised and flexible rather than relying on a single approach. Online delivery and provisions for pacing and rest were requested by participants. The reported diagnostic difficulties and inconsistent advice also indicate potential value in improving healthcare professionals’ awareness of ANOCA and coordinating guidance. These are implications raised by the talk, not tested interventions.

LIMITATIONS AND UNCERTAINTIES
The results were preliminary, and the talk did not provide the total number of participants or detailed demographic information. Findings were based on participant reports and do not establish the safety or effectiveness of a particular exercise prescription. The speaker reported three male participants and said the group included more women; the audience discussion did not establish the study’s exact gender breakdown.

AUDIENCE QUESTIONS
Asked whether the female-majority group reflected the population, the speaker said research suggests approximately 60% of people with ANOCA are female and 40% male. She noted that some women described fear around discussing difficult experiences and that the three male participants also provided valuable accounts.

FOLLOW-UP READING
No specific publications or further reading were named in the talk.
notes.speaker: Kayleigh Jarrett, Paul A Swinton, Stephen J Leslie, Andy Hall

notes.title: Closing the Gap: A Rapid-Start, Digitally Supported Cardiac Rehabilitation Pathway Improves Early Engagement and Uptake
notes.summary:
OVERVIEW
Angela, a lead cardiac nurse at CPLR, described a retrospective evaluation of whether reducing delays to cardiac rehabilitation could improve initial attendance and continued engagement. The study covered 291 patients enrolled during 2025.

MAIN ARGUMENTS
The speaker argued that delays after referral may weaken engagement, lead to early dropout, or make attendance harder as people return to work and normal activities. Their service aimed to contact and assess people promptly, offer virtual or in-person assessment, and minimize the gap between assessment and starting exercise.

KEY FINDINGS
The speaker reported that 97% attended a first assessment, compared with a cited national average of 44.5%. A reported 82% proceeded to a second assessment; the speaker said this was comparable to the national average. Referral-to-assessment time was reported as 28 days for CABG patients and 20 days for MI patients; the speaker described these as better than the national average. The transcript does not provide the corresponding national wait-time figures or a result for completion of the full 12-week program.

METHODS OR EVIDENCE
This was a retrospective review of existing data over 2025; the speaker said the service did not change anything during the study period. The pathway included administrative contact within 48 hours, a Zoom conversation, and an initial assessment offered virtually or in person. The service aimed to start exercise within a few days, or within a week if not possible sooner. In-person assessment could include treadmill or bicycle CPET. For virtual assessment, the speaker described sit-to-stand and a walk test, with a heart-rate strap used to show heart rate live on Zoom. Measures mentioned in response to questions included cholesterol, glucose, blood pressure, and resting heart rate. The transcript’s reference to “two maps” is unclear.

PRACTICAL OR CLINICAL IMPLICATIONS
The speaker recommended considering faster contact and assessment, flexible virtual access, and reducing the delay between assessment and exercise. These are features of the service described; the retrospective findings do not establish that any one feature caused the reported attendance rates. The service has centers in Bath and London, and virtual appointments were presented as an option for people facing travel barriers.

LIMITATIONS AND UNCERTAINTIES
The study covered one provider and was retrospective. The speaker said the review could not account for people missed before referral or people the service could not contact at first outreach. Functional and cost outcomes were not evaluated in this analysis, though functional-outcome data were planned for a future project. The transcript does not clarify the denominator for the 82% figure, provide detailed national comparators, or report full 12-week completion. The speaker also proposed examining virtual versus in-person pathways and other UK services in future work.

AUDIENCE QUESTIONS
Audience members asked which virtual platform and functional measures were used, how virtual testing supported risk stratification, and whether patients received heart-rate monitors. The speaker said Zoom was used for most patients; virtual tests included sit-to-stand and a walk test, and patients received a heart-rate strap whose readings could be viewed live by the patient and exercise specialist. In-person tests could include treadmill or bicycle CPET.

FOLLOW-UP READING
No publications or other reading were cited in the talk.

notes.title: Health inequalities and women's health
notes.summary:
OVERVIEW
The conference and speaker were not identified in the supplied transcript. This talk discusses sex-specific cardiovascular risks, presentation, and prevention across women’s lives.

MAIN ARGUMENTS
The speaker argues that cardiovascular disease in women is under-recognized, despite being a major cause of death. Biological factors—including pregnancy, menopause, and differences in atherosclerosis—as well as psychosocial factors can affect risk and care. The speaker calls for stronger prevention and consideration of more aggressive risk-factor management for women, while noting that appropriate targets remain uncertain.

KEY FINDINGS
The speaker stated that 3.6 million women are affected by ischemic heart disease, that 30% of myocardial infarctions occur in women, and that women are twice as likely to die from cardiovascular disease as from breast cancer. The talk emphasized that smoking, diabetes, and obesity may carry greater cardiovascular risk in women than in men, and that some women experience cardiovascular events without recognized conventional risk factors.

Pregnancy-related hypertension and gestational diabetes were presented as markers of future cardiovascular risk. The speaker cited a 45% higher coronary artery disease risk after gestational diabetes compared with an age-matched person without it. Takotsubo syndrome was described as predominantly affecting women, especially after menopause; microvascular angina was also described as more common in women.

METHODS OR EVIDENCE
The talk was a narrative presentation, referring to Framingham findings, a large US study of hormone replacement therapy (HRT), research on sex differences in atherosclerosis, and a British Heart Foundation publication about pregnancy complications. No study methods, full citations, or detailed data were provided in the transcript. The speaker described estrogen-related cardiovascular effects and argued that HRT findings depend in part on timing and dose, referring to initiation within 10 years—preferably within five—of menopause.

PRACTICAL OR CLINICAL IMPLICATIONS
The speaker encouraged clinicians to ask about pregnancy complications when assessing cardiovascular risk and to consider increased surveillance, education, and risk-factor modification for affected women. The talk also urged attention to sex-specific symptoms and conditions, including microvascular angina. HRT comments were general statements from the talk, not individualized treatment guidance.

LIMITATIONS AND UNCERTAINTIES
Several statistics and study references lack enough detail in the transcript to verify their definitions, populations, or context. The speaker acknowledged that evidence does not yet settle whether women need different prevention targets, and noted uncertainty about sex differences in how often microvascular angina causes symptoms or presents clinically. The talk did not provide a systematic review or enough information to assess the cited HRT evidence in detail.

AUDIENCE QUESTIONS
No audience questions or answers appear in the transcript. The closing remarks mention submitting questions through Slido, but no event code or responses are available.

FOLLOW-UP READING
The transcript does not provide complete citations. Useful sources to identify from the speaker’s references would include the Framingham study, the US HRT study discussed, and the British Heart Foundation publication on pregnancy complications and cardiovascular risk.
notes.speaker: Dr Dawn Adamson
notes.verification_note: The summary title is not the programme title; the match is based on the summary’s focus on cardiovascular disease in women and the programme’s women’s health presentation.

notes.title: Bridging the Gap: Reducing Inequalities in Cardiac Rehabilitation Through Innovation and System Change
notes.summary:
OVERVIEW
The speaker argues that cardiac rehabilitation is beneficial but remains inaccessible to many eligible people. The talk focuses on using service redesign, digital tools and system-wide collaboration to improve access without treating technology as a replacement for clinical expertise. The speaker is introduced as Nicola Bowis and later self-identifies as Nick Bowis; the transcript gives both names.

MAIN ARGUMENTS
• Inequity can arise from pathway failures, including missed referrals, travel and caring responsibilities, language barriers, and services that do not suit patients’ circumstances or cultures.
• Digital innovation can widen access, but poorly implemented technology can create new barriers. Offer digital, hybrid and non-digital choices.
• Build equity into service design from the start, involve patients, connect acute and community care, and share learning about both successful and unsuccessful approaches.
• Technology and data should support clinicians and patients, not replace their expertise.

KEY FINDINGS
• The speaker reports that a local digital platform enabling automatic cardiac rehabilitation referrals increased programme entry, more than doubled completion compared with the previous service, exceeded the cited national average for completion, reduced median time to entry, and reduced six-month cardiac readmissions. Exact figures and statistical details were not provided.
• A later multi-trust education app had uneven clinician engagement across sites and was difficult to implement. The speaker cited activation emails being missed, staff workload, training and governance as barriers.
• In a separate lipid-optimisation programme, about 10,000 people with non-optimised LDL were identified; 4,596 received a telephone consultation, more than 1,000 started injectable therapies, and 41 GP practices were onboarded.

METHODS OR EVIDENCE
The talk drew on local service redesign involving relevant stakeholders, a comparison of 350 patients receiving the previous referral process with patients using automatic digital referrals, and the speaker’s implementation experience. It also described patient feedback and involvement through focus groups and PPI, alongside the lipid-optimisation programme. The transcript refers to publications and awards but does not provide citations or detailed study methods.

PRACTICAL OR CLINICAL IMPLICATIONS
• Systematically identify eligible patients and make referrals reliable rather than dependent on informal processes.
• Design flexible pathways around patients’ lives and connect hospital, primary care, community and voluntary-sector support.
• Provide suitable face-to-face, remote, hybrid and non-digital options; assess digital barriers rather than assuming who will or will not use technology.
• Use population data to examine who is not being reached, including by gender, ethnicity, geography and deprivation, and ask patients what would make services usable.
• Treat implementation, workforce capacity, training, governance and ongoing evaluation as part of the intervention.

LIMITATIONS AND UNCERTAINTIES
The transcript does not give detailed methods, exact effect sizes, statistical analyses, patient characteristics or equity-stratified outcomes for the cardiac rehabilitation comparison. The reported local results therefore do not establish how readily the approach would generalise elsewhere. The app experience demonstrates implementation challenges but is not presented with a formal evaluation. The original referral platform was described as outdated and in need of upgrades, including better links with primary care and wearables. The transcript does not establish the impact of the lipid programme on longer-term clinical outcomes.

AUDIENCE QUESTIONS
The Q&A begins with an audience member asking whether women-specific cardiovascular risk models are being developed. The transcript cuts off before the question is completed or answered; no other audience questions are captured.

FOLLOW-UP READING
No specific papers, reports or links are named in the transcript. The speaker recommends publishing and sharing evidence, including learning from approaches that did not work.

notes.title: Digital – get it right first time
notes.summary:
OVERVIEW
Rajiv Sankaranarayanan, a consultant cardiologist and heart failure lead, discussed how home digital cardiac rehabilitation might improve access to rehabilitation for people with heart failure. He presented background evidence, NICE’s early value assessment, and evaluations of two digital platforms. Digital options were described as additional choices, not replacements for conventional rehabilitation.

MAIN ARGUMENTS
• Cardiac rehabilitation benefits people with heart failure, yet referral and uptake remain low; the speaker cited UK uptake of around 15% or less and a study in which only 1.6% of eligible patients received rehabilitation.
• Hospital-based delivery can create travel, staffing, time, and infrastructure barriers, with unequal access reported for women, older people, ethnic minorities, and people living in deprived areas.
• Digital home delivery may make rehabilitation more accessible and flexible. It should be offered alongside conventional rehabilitation, following professional assessment and discussion of suitability, safety, and patient preference.
• NICE’s early value assessment conditionally recommended seven technologies for NHS use during a three-year evidence-generation period. The speaker emphasized that evidence is not yet sufficient to establish routine adoption.

KEY FINDINGS
• The speaker cited systematic reviews and meta-analyses reporting improvements in mortality, heart-failure hospitalizations or readmissions, exercise capacity, and quality of life across reduced and preserved ejection fraction. He also described research involving more than 40,000 patients, reporting reductions of 42% in all-cause mortality, 26% in hospitalization, 53% in incident atrial fibrillation, and 37% in incident stroke; the transcript does not provide the study’s full methods or citation.
• For the Pumping Marvellous platform, a preprint covering 673 registrants (August 2024–July 2025) reportedly found that nearly 63% were women; around one-third had heart failure with mildly reduced ejection fraction; about 6% were from minority ethnic communities; and only 6% had previously participated in cardiac rehabilitation. The speaker also cited later, unpublished data indicating around 2,000 users and that 70% had never previously been offered rehabilitation.
• In an evaluation following discharge from a heart-failure ward, 185 patients were referred to a home digital programme; 116 (63%) took it up, compared with 10% for standard cardiac rehabilitation, and the reported completion rate was 70%. The speaker reported lower readmission rates in the digital-programme cohort—76% lower at 30 days and 70% lower at 90 days—and improvements in activity, quality of life, self-efficacy, and mental well-being. These are reported evaluation results, not proof that the programme caused the differences.

METHODS OR EVIDENCE
The talk drew on published meta-analyses and systematic reviews, research cited by the speaker, NICE’s evidence review, a preprint using platform registration data, unpublished platform data, and a digital rehabilitation evaluation conducted from May 2024 to February 2025. The latter involved referral after hospital discharge, a wearable activity monitor, a personalized online dashboard, and six 20-minute calls with a trained mentor; outcomes were assessed at 30 and 90 days against standard care. The transcript does not give full study designs, citations, or statistical details for all results.

PRACTICAL OR CLINICAL IMPLICATIONS
• Refer eligible patients promptly rather than treating rehabilitation as an afterthought.
• Offer both conventional and digital home-based options, with trained-professional assessment and shared, personalized decision-making.
• Support patient and carer onboarding; train staff; integrate digital programmes with local rehabilitation pathways and data collection.
• Monitor whether digital delivery reduces or worsens inequities, including barriers related to digital access, culture, ethnicity, and religion.
• Generate comparative evidence on clinical outcomes, uptake, cost, staff time, data requirements, and implementation during NICE’s three-year evidence-generation period.

LIMITATIONS AND UNCERTAINTIES
NICE’s review found limited and uncertain comparisons with conventional rehabilitation: studies had short follow-up (none longer than six months, as described in the talk), varied outcome definitions, and limited evidence on adverse events and hospitalizations. The platform evaluations were presented as early evidence; the transcript does not establish randomized allocation or provide enough methodological detail to assess confounding and selection effects. Some platform names and phrases are unclear in the transcript, and the later Pumping Marvellous figures were explicitly described as unpublished.

AUDIENCE QUESTIONS
No audience questions or answers appear in the transcript. The moderator invited attendees to submit and upvote questions through Slido for a planned Q&A.

FOLLOW-UP READING
• NICE HealthTech guidance HTG 761 on digital technologies for cardiac rehabilitation, cited in the talk; the transcript does not give the full document title or publication date.
• The Pumping Marvellous platform preprint described by the speaker; no full citation is provided in the transcript.

notes.title: Beyond the Technology: Building Future-Ready Cardiac Rehabilitation Through Data, Digital and AI
notes.summary:
OVERVIEW
Katrina, a pharmacist by background and project manager at the North London Cardiac Operational Delivery Network, discussed how data-led service improvement can support cardiac rehabilitation and how digital tools and narrow AI might help address workload and access challenges. She emphasized that technology should solve defined service problems, support patient care, and be introduced with appropriate governance.

MAIN ARGUMENTS
- AI is already used in healthcare and other everyday settings; the speaker focused on narrow AI, not human-like general AI.
- Healthcare adoption is slower than in some other sectors, but caution about patient safety should not become paralysis. Claims about AI should be tested against meaningful outcomes and timeframes.
- Service improvement should start with the problem and workflow, not with a particular app or AI product. Some improvements may come from reducing friction and duplication without AI.
- Digital and AI-enabled care should complement clinical teams and preserve a non-digital option.

KEY FINDINGS
- The network supported an increase from eight to 14 cardiac rehabilitation services meeting certification requirements over several years.
- In North East London, heart-failure-related cardiac rehabilitation uptake was reported at about 22%, against a stated 33% national ask. The transcript’s wording for that ask is unclear.
- The pathway review identified teams using separate spreadsheets as a practical barrier. The speaker also highlighted that some patients with HFpEF may not be diagnosed by heart-failure teams, affecting their route into rehabilitation.
- A digital-pathway workshop produced proposed must-have requirements. The speaker highlighted non-digital access, clinical governance, and early clinical-team involvement.

METHODS OR EVIDENCE
- The speaker described a five-year improvement journey, including alignment with cardiac rehabilitation standards and NHS priorities.
- For certification work, the network used national and local data to identify gaps and secured NHS England funding.
- For the North East London heart failure pathway, the team conducted a multidisciplinary review, held workshops, used fishbone analysis to examine barriers, and prioritized quick wins and longer-term changes.
- The network was developing digital-pathway requirements through evidence review, pathway review, and stakeholder engagement. A workshop guide was said to be available on the Future NHS site.
- The speaker cited examples of AI use, including scan highlighting, ambient note-taking, and research using routine ECGs to detect signs of heart failure and valve disease. Specific studies or performance data were not provided in the transcript.

PRACTICAL OR CLINICAL IMPLICATIONS
- Review referral, reminder, form, and information-sharing processes; reduce duplicate data entry and administrative work where possible.
- Consider digital support across identification and referral, assessment and onboarding, programme delivery, and ongoing review, while ensuring clinical decisions remain appropriately governed.
- Before introducing a tool, ask: What specific problem are we solving? Who is accountable if it goes wrong? Does it fit the current workflow?
- The speaker suggested using available tools such as Copilot for tasks like meeting notes, email editing, or preliminary evidence scanning, but not as a substitute for a proper literature review.

LIMITATIONS AND UNCERTAINTIES
- The transcript provides no detailed outcome data, study citations, dates, denominators, or evaluation methods for the service-improvement examples or the AI claims.
- The stated 33% national uptake ask is repeated with unclear wording, and the transcript does not specify the time period or how uptake was calculated.
- The speaker’s comparison of healthcare adoption with leading sectors is not accompanied by the graph’s source or underlying figures.
- The digital-pathway requirements were described as being developed; effectiveness and implementation outcomes were not reported.
- The talk advocates governed adoption, but does not establish that any particular AI tool improves cardiac rehabilitation outcomes.

AUDIENCE QUESTIONS
No audience questions or answers are included in the transcript. The speaker posed rhetorical questions about everyday use of algorithms and asked attendees to consider the problem, accountability, and workflow fit before adopting a tool.

FOLLOW-UP READING
- The European Society of Cardiology’s dedicated cardiac rehabilitation guidelines, which the speaker said recommend digital health, AI, and tele-rehabilitation models for most patients; the exact guideline citation was not provided.
- The speaker’s blog and two-page digital-pathway guide on the Future NHS site.
- Resources from the NHS AI Ambassador Network.
- Work and commentary by AI ethicist Dr Jessica Morley, as referenced by the speaker.

notes.title: Modern Service Framework – What the Data Shows Us for the Future
notes.summary:
OVERVIEW
Dr Alex Harrison presented an analysis of current cardiac rehabilitation (CR) service performance and the challenges of increasing uptake in England. The slides were developed with Patrick Doherty, who could not attend. The talk considered progress, the 2036 uptake target, potential barriers and how service data could guide improvement.

MAIN ARGUMENTS
- CR services have improved their certification performance, but reaching the national uptake target will require continued improvement and sustained capacity.
- Increasing access requires addressing inequalities, identifying underserved and high-risk groups, and offering varied delivery options suited to patients’ needs.
- Local data should help services and health-system leaders identify barriers such as long waits, distance, language needs and workforce pressures.
- Accurate, complete data entry is essential to describe services’ performance and support local business cases and national planning.

KEY FINDINGS
- This year, 59% of services were green certified and about one-third were amber; 8% were red and one service failed. Ninety-five programmes maintained green status from the previous year, 22 services newly achieved it, and 35 programmes moved up at least one status.
- The speaker reported that 96% of services had at least three professional disciplines and 91% included all priority groups named in the talk: myocardial infarction, revascularisation and heart failure patients.
- The Modern Service Framework target cited was to raise CR uptake from a baseline of about 45% to 70% over ten years, with an interim target of 55% after three years.
- Uptake was reported to be 9 percentage points lower for patients from the most deprived areas than for those from the least deprived areas.
- For the myocardial infarction/percutaneous coronary intervention waiting-time measure, the reported median was 18 days and the target cited was 33 days. The speaker said 83% of services met the target, 17% did not, and 7% had median waits above 55 days; 13 programmes had median waits above 55 days.
- The speaker estimated that, if the eligible denominator stayed constant, quarterly attendance would need to rise from 7,200 in 2025–26 quarter two to about 10,000 to reach 70% uptake. He described this as requiring roughly 3,000 additional patients per quarter at the target level, or a staged increase of about 85 additional patients per quarter across programmes.
- In the workforce survey, nearly half of services reported permanent staff departures and 60% reported at least one temporary staff absence. Fewer than 30% reported trying to recruit an additional post; 150 teams did not try, and 10 tried but were unsuccessful.

METHODS OR EVIDENCE
The presentation drew on NACR service certification and performance data, service survey responses, and dashboard and geographical mapping examples. It also referred to reported group, home and hybrid delivery patterns, NHS dashboard comparisons, and an ONS estimate that one million people have English-limiting language skills. These were primarily descriptive findings; the talk did not present causal analyses or detailed study methods.

PRACTICAL OR CLINICAL IMPLICATIONS
- Review local uptake and certification indicators to identify where access or waiting times need attention, and share learning between services.
- Consider patient choice and needs when offering group, home, hybrid or digital rehabilitation; design accessibility and language support in from the outset.
- Examine whether distance, transport, employment, caring responsibilities, digital access, communication needs or frailty may affect participation, and tailor engagement accordingly.
- Plan for workforce resilience and capacity, including whether upskilling may help where recruitment is difficult.
- Maintain complete data entry so services’ needs and progress can be represented in local and national planning.

LIMITATIONS AND UNCERTAINTIES
- The speaker noted that the uptake denominator may change, so projections assuming it remains static are conditional.
- The dataset described does not include a frailty score or a direct measure of English-language ability. Ethnicity was mentioned only as an imperfect proxy for possible local language-support needs.
- The reported figures describe service performance and survey responses; they do not establish that any particular intervention will cause uptake to rise.
- The talk identified several possible barriers but noted that more detailed understanding is needed about which patient subgroups are not attending and why.

AUDIENCE QUESTIONS
No audience questions or discussion were included in the transcript.

FOLLOW-UP READING
No specific publications were named. The talk referred to the cardiovascular disease Modern Service Framework, NACR certification and performance reporting, the NHS Model Health System/Model Hospital dashboard, and ONS language data.

notes.title: From Patients to People: Social Prescribing, the Missing Link in Cardiac Rehabilitation
notes.summary:
OVERVIEW
Anna, a cardiac rehabilitation specialist nurse, and Sharon, a social prescriber at University Hospitals Coventry and Warwickshire, described an 18-month pilot integrating social prescribing into cardiac rehabilitation. Their central concern was whether patients’ wider social circumstances and barriers to access were being addressed alongside their clinical needs.

MAIN ARGUMENTS
Cardiac recovery is shaped by more than diagnosis and treatment: financial strain, transport, housing, isolation, employment and other circumstances can affect a person’s ability to engage with rehabilitation. The speakers argued that placing social prescribing within cardiac rehab can make existing community support more accessible, particularly for people in deprived communities, while also strengthening the clinical team’s ability to respond to non-clinical needs.

KEY FINDINGS
• 74% of referrals were for patients living in the two most deprived IMD quintiles (quintiles 1 and 2); 61% of referrals related to financial support. Other needs included mental health, social isolation, employment, caring responsibilities and wider welfare support.
• In patient feedback, 100% of respondents said they would not otherwise have accessed social prescribing. 86% said it had helped their overall wellbeing, and more than half felt it helped them stay engaged with or attend cardiac rehabilitation.
• In a staff survey, 100% of respondents felt the social prescriber benefited patients and was valuable to the service; 100% felt the role reduced clinical staff time spent addressing non-clinical issues. Staff also reported greater confidence and knowledge of community support.
• A patient example illustrated how a referral for help with a Personal Independence Payment application also led to support for the patient’s financially struggling carer.

METHODS OR EVIDENCE
The team built on a service-improvement project that had identified deprivation-related inequalities in uptake and completion, and a lack of a structured pathway for non-clinical needs. They introduced a social prescriber for 15 hours per week, offering up to 12 weeks of individualised support, with referrals possible at any stage of cardiac rehabilitation. The talk drew on referral patterns, patient and staff feedback surveys, and a patient case example. Coventry context included an estimated population of about 345,000, around 45% of residents from ethnic minority groups, and household fuel poverty estimated at almost one in four in 2022, rising above 40% in some deprived communities.

PRACTICAL OR CLINICAL IMPLICATIONS
An embedded social prescriber can assess what matters to a patient, make referrals directly to community or voluntary organisations, and follow up to help patients access support. This may reduce the burden of navigating services alone and allow clinical staff to focus more on clinical care. The speakers presented this as a potential way to improve equity of access and support recovery in the context of patients’ lives.

LIMITATIONS AND UNCERTAINTIES
The pilot is ongoing, and the talk did not provide survey sample sizes, detailed outcome measures, a comparison group, or evidence that the service caused changes in rehabilitation completion or cardiovascular outcomes. The speakers noted that existing integrated mental health support means the social-prescribing referral data may not reflect the full mental health need in their population. Findings are early and specific to this service context.

AUDIENCE QUESTIONS
The transcript ends with an incomplete, unclear audience remark about social prescribing. No complete question or substantive answer is captured.

FOLLOW-UP READING
No publications, reports or other follow-up reading were named in the talk.
